newsitem.title: USA: Insurers' performance tied to customer retention.
newsitem.headline: Insurers' performance tied to customer retention.

text.p: Insurance companies that hold on to existing policyholders year after year tend to have better financial results than their competitors, according to a study released on Sunday.
The study by consulting firm Tillinghast-Towers Perrin included 17 major insurers with a personal lines market share of about 35 percent.

"Retention (of customers) matters," said Jamie Pickles, a managing consultant with Tillinghast-Towers Perin. "Personal lines companies that have superior retention results will gain a competitive advantage in the marketplace."
Companies with high customer retention rates in both standard auto and homeowners on average had better financial results than companies with lower retention rates, he said.
The standard auto combined ratio for top-tier performers was about five points lower than that of lower-tier participants he said.
The combined ratio indicates whether a company is earning a profit on the business it writes. An underwriting profit occurs when the ratio is below 100 percent.
Market share also is an important factor in customer retention, the study found.
In 13 out of 17 cases, the participant's largest state had a higher retention ratio than the participant's countrywide average.
"A state's significance to a participant may lead to increased company attention, which could be helping renewal retention," Pickles said.
The study also found twelve-month policies had better customer retention than six-month policies for both standard non-standard auto.
In addition, customer retention results for non-standard auto were substantially lower than for standard auto.
And tenants/condo owners' policies retention ratio was more than 10 points lower than that for owners' policies.

The study was intended to help personal lines insurers better understand policyholder retention measures used in the industry, to benchmark their retention performance against other companies and to identify best practices that lead to improved retention performance.

"We found that some companies are more focused and therefore mroe effective than others at measuring retention and instituting practices that address the issues," said Bruce Bassman, a Tillinghast-Towers Perrin principal.

"Clearly there are operational improvements that will translate into better retention experience for companies. However, some of these improvements will require an investment that will impact short-term financial results," Bassman said.
An additional study, with an expanded group of participants is scheduled for 1997.
